abstract: Stanford HAI's 2026 AI Index Report provides a comprehensive annual assessment of AI's progress and societal impact, with notable findings on employment, adoption, and healthcare. The report documents that employment among software developers aged 22-25 has plummeted nearly 20% since 2024, even as headcount among their older colleagues continues to grow—a striking pattern that repeats in other occupations with higher levels of AI exposure, such as customer service. This age-stratified employment effect suggests AI may be disproportionately affecting entry-level positions while preserving or expanding demand for experienced workers. On adoption, generative AI reached 53% population adoption within three years, faster than the personal computer or the internet, though the US ranks only 24th globally at 28.3% adoption. In healthcare, physicians across multiple hospital systems reported up to 83% less time spent writing notes and significant reductions in burnout, demonstrating concrete productivity gains from AI integration in professional settings.
keyFindings: Employment among software developers aged 22-25 has dropped nearly 20% since 2024, while older developers' headcount continues growing—a pattern repeated in other AI-exposed occupations like customer service.
Generative AI reached 53% population adoption within three years globally, faster than personal computers or the internet achieved comparable penetration.
The US ranks only 24th globally in AI adoption at 28.3%, despite being a leading AI development hub.
Physicians across multiple hospital systems reported up to 83% less time spent writing clinical notes and significant reductions in burnout from AI adoption.

The age-stratified employment effect—declining entry-level hiring with stable or growing experienced headcount—suggests AI is compressing the bottom of occupational ladders rather than eliminating entire job categories.
methodology: Annual comprehensive analysis compiled by Stanford HAI drawing on multiple data sources including Bureau of Labor Statistics employment data (age-stratified), global adoption surveys, healthcare system outcome studies, and industry benchmarks. The AI Index aggregates data from academic institutions, government agencies, and industry sources worldwide. Software developer employment analysis uses CPS microdata stratified by age cohorts. Adoption data from multi-country population surveys. Healthcare data from implementations across multiple hospital systems.
qualifiers: The 20% decline in young developer employment coincides with broader tech sector layoffs and hiring freezes (2024-2026), making causal attribution to AI specifically difficult. Adoption metrics vary significantly by definition—the 53% global figure and 28.3% US figure may use different criteria. Healthcare productivity gains are measured in specific hospital systems that may have been early adopters or particularly well-suited for AI integration. The AI Index is a compilation and synthesis rather than original research, and individual findings carry the limitations of their underlying studies. Country ranking methodology may not capture informal or embedded AI usage.
